The African wild dog, Lycaon pictus, is a highly social canid whose life-history parameters reflect its cooperative breeding system. Birth mass in this species is notably modest, with neonates weighing approximately 318 grams [Wwb = approximately 318 grams] at parturition, a value that underscores the altricial state of the newborn pups. Under the thermoneutral body temperature typical of active canids (38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]), the gestation period lasts 72 days [tg = 72 days], a duration consistent with that of other large-bodied pack-hunting canids. This relatively short intrauterine development period, compared to solitary canids of similar mass, is likely facilitated by the extensive postnatal care provided by the entire pack, which includes regurgitation of food and protection of the litter at the den site. The combination of a modest birth mass and a tightly constrained gestation interval suggests an evolutionary strategy that prioritizes rapid offspring production over extended prenatal development, relying instead on the buffering effects of communal rearing to enhance pup survival.

Female African wild dogs achieve an ultimate body mass of approximately 26,500 grams [Wwi = approximately 26,500 grams], placing them squarely within the broader adult mass range of 18 to 36 kilograms reported for the species. This substantial adult size is ecologically linked to their cursorial hunting strategy, which requires sustained aerobic endurance over long chases through African savanna habitats. Following parturition at the 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] internal body temperature characteristic of the species, the developmental trajectory is tightly scheduled. The weaning period, representing the transition from complete milk dependency to the initial ingestion of regurgitated solid food, occurs at 91 days since birth [tx = 91 days since birth] at a temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This relatively extended nursing phase, when compared to smaller canids, reflects the energetic demands of rapid skeletal growth in a species that must attain sufficient body size to participate effectively in cooperative hunts by late juvenility.

Puberty in Lycaon pictus, marking the onset of reproductive physiological capacity, is reached at 639 days since birth [tp = 639 days since birth], a value recorded under the typical core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This extended pre-reproductive period, spanning nearly two years, is among the longest documented for canids of comparable adult mass and is intimately linked to the species' social system. In wild populations, subordinate individuals often delay actual breeding even beyond physiological maturity due to reproductive suppression by the dominant pair, meaning that the age of first reproduction in the field frequently exceeds the intrinsic pubertal milestone reported here from captive studies. The long interval between weaning and puberty provides ample time for young dogs to acquire the sophisticated hunting and territorial skills necessary for successful pack integration and eventual reproductive dominance.

The species exhibits a modest annual reproductive output despite its potential for higher fecundity. Reproductive data indicate that female African wild dogs produce a single litter each year, with each litter containing eight pups on average, yielding a total of eight pups per year [Ri = eight pups per year] per breeding female. This rate is substantially lower than the theoretical maximum for a canid of this body size. The constraint is imposed not by physiological limits but by the ecological demands of cooperative pup-rearing, where the availability of auxiliary helpers and the seasonal abundance of prey govern the optimal litter size. Field observations confirm that packs with more adult helpers consistently rear a higher proportion of pups to weaning age, underscoring the social regulation of reproductive output in this obligate cooperative breeder.

Comparative longevity data for Lycaon pictus, derived from longitudinal field studies and captive records, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] when measured at the standard mammalian core temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C]. This translates to roughly 6,205 days, placing the African wild dog among the longer-lived canids relative to its body size, though shorter than the extreme lifespans documented in some domestic dog breeds. The species' extended lifespan is notable given the high extrinsic mortality rates faced by wild populations from interspecific competition with lions and hyenas, as well as from habitat fragmentation and disease outbreaks. From a life-history perspective, the combination of a long lifespan, delayed puberty, and a low annual reproductive rate aligns with a slow pace-of-life syndrome typical of large, socially complex carnivores that invest heavily in offspring care and intra-pack cooperation.
